claim: TRPC3 is most prominently expressed in the olivocerebellar circuit in the normal mouse brain, specifically in Purkinje cells (PCs) and unipolar brush cells (UBCs).
source: We found that in the normal mouse brain TRPC3 is most prominently expressed in the olivocerebellar circuit (Figure 1A), specifically in PCs and unipolar brush cells (UBCs) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1A and 1B showing TRPC3 expression patterns in mouse brain.

claim: Endogenous TRPC3 is not distributed homogeneously in Purkinje cells, with higher levels in the anterior cerebellum (predominantly Z-) than in the posterior cerebellum (primarily Z+).
source: Upon further scrutiny it is clear that, although expressed in all PCs, endogenous TRPC3 was not distributed homogeneously. The TRPC3 levels in the anterior cerebellum, where the PCs are predominantly Z–, were higher than those in the posterior PCs, which are primarily Z+ (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and quantification shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRPC3 expression is complementary to Zebrin II in the vermis, while in the hemispheres TRPC3 expression varies between homogeneous expression and expression complementary to Zebrin II.
source: This analysis confirmed that TRPC3 expression is complementary to that of Zebrin in the vermis, while in the hemispheres the TRPC3 expression varies between homogeneous expression and expression complementary to Zebrin II.
evidence: The claim is based on quantification of relative levels of TRPC3 and Zebrin II in several subregions as shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The anterior/posterior differences in TRPC3 protein amount were confirmed by western blot analysis.
source: The anterior/posterior differences in the protein amount were confirmed by western blot analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: TRPC3 is present in the soma and dendritic arbor of Purkinje cells.
source: Our immunohistochemical imaging reveals that TRPC3 is present in the soma and dendritic arbor of PCs (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: TRPC3 is abundantly present in the membrane and almost completely absent in the cytosol.
source: As expected, TRPC3, a channel protein, is abundantly present in the membrane and almost completely absent in the cytosol (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data of isolated fractions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: TRPC3 is enriched in synaptosomes.
source: Moreover, TRPC3 is enriched in synapstosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), in line with the common conception of mGluR1b-dependent activation of TRPC3 (Hartmann et al., 2008; Ohtani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D and is consistent with previous literature on mGluR1b-dependent activation of TRPC3.

claim: TRPC3-Moonwalker (TRPC3Mwk/-) mice harbor a point mutation resulting in TRPC3 gain-of-function through increased Ca2+ influx upon activation.
source: TRPC3-Moonwalker (TRPC3Mwk/-) mice harbor a point mutation resulting in TRPC3 gain-of-function through increased Ca2+ influx upon activation (Becker et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Becker et al., 2009 describing the TRPC3Mwk/- mouse model.

claim: TRPC3-Moonwalker mice are featured by neurodegeneration, first of UBCs and later also of PCs, and display early onset ataxia.
source: These mice are featured by neurodegeneration, first of UBCs and later also of PCs, and as a consequence display early onset ataxia (Sekerková et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Sekerková et al., 2013 describing the phenotype of TRPC3Mwk/- mice.

claim: pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice exhibited no overt signs of ataxia or other movement deficits upon visual inspection.
source: These pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice exhibited no overt signs of ataxia or other movement deficits upon visual inspection.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection observations of the pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.

claim: Western blotting and immunostaining of the anterior (Z-) and the posterior (Z+) cerebellar cortex of pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice confirmed that TRPC3 protein levels are reduced.
source: Western blotting and immunostaining of the anterior (Z–) and the posterior (Z+) cerebellar cortex of pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice confirmed that TRPC3 protein levels are reduced, without disrupting the typical zebrin staining pattern (WB, anterior: t19=2.63, p=0.034; posterior: t19 = 2.67, p=0.028) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B,E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting and immunostaining data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B,E-F.

claim: The loss of TRPC3 in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice was specific for cerebellar PCs, as TRPC3 expression in UBCs was not affected.
source: The loss of TRPC3 was specific for cerebellar PCs, as TRPC3 expression in UBCs was not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F, white arrow heads).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F demonstrating TRPC3 expression in UBCs.

claim: In littermate controls, the intrinsic firing rate of Z- PCs is higher than that of Z+ PCs.
source: In littermate controls, the intrinsic firing rate of Z– PCs is higher than that of Z+ PCs, confirming previous results (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiological recordings and is consistent with previous findings from Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: Gain-of-function TRPC3Mwk/- mice showed an increase in PC simple spike firing rate selectively in Z- PCs (84.5 ± 36.2 Hz vs. 58.4 ± 19.6 Hz for mutants vs. controls; t19 = -2.47, p=0.020), without affecting Z+ PCs (36.7 ± 13.0 Hz vs. 39.7 ± 21.5 Hz for mutants vs. controls t21=0.419, p=0.680).
source: Gain-of-function TRPC3Mwk/- mice showed an increase in PC simple spike firing rate selectively in Z– PCs (84.5 ± 36.2 Hz vs. 58.4 ± 19.6 Hz for mutants vs. controls; t19 = −2.47, p=0.020), without affecting Z+ PCs (36.7 ± 13.0 Hz vs. 39.7 ± 21.5 Hz for mutants vs. controls t21=0.419, p=0.680) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro cell-attached recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ablating TRPC3 from PCs caused a decrease in firing rate in Z- PCs (44.1 ± 15.6 Hz vs. 55.4 ± 21.8 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t81=2.69, p=0.009), without affecting Z+ PCs (28.5 ± 9.3 Hz vs. 30.8 ± 11.7 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t64=0.937, p=0.352).
source: Inversely, ablating TRPC3 from PCs caused a decrease in firing rate in Z– PCs (44.1 ± 15.6 Hz vs. 55.4 ± 21.8 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t81=2.69, p=0.009), again without affecting Z+ PCs (28.5 ± 9.3 Hz vs. 30.8 ± 11.7 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t64=0.937, p=0.352) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro cell-attached recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the absence of TRPC3, the firing rate of Z- PCs does not drop to the levels of Z+ PCs, suggesting that TRPC3 provides a major, but not exclusive, contribution to the difference.
source: However, in the absence of TRPC3 the firing rate of Z– PCs does not drop to the levels of Z+ PCs, suggesting that TRPC3 provides a major, but not exclusive, contribution to the difference.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the firing rate data comparing Z- and Z+ PCs in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.

claim: Both the CV and CV2 of Z- PCs in lobules I-III declined significantly in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice, while remaining unchanged in TRPC3Mwk/- mice.
source: Both the CV and CV2 of Z– PCs in lobules I-III declined significantly in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice, while remaining unchanged in TRPC3Mwk/- mice; in contrast, in Z+ lobule X, none of these parameters were altered in either TRPC3Mwk/- or pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of firing regularity parameters shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: In loss-of-function pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice, PC intrinsic excitability was significantly reduced in lobules I-III (16.0 ± 1.0 Hz/100 pA vs. 19.2 ± 1.1 Hz/100 pA, mut. vs. ctrl, t32=-2.20, p=0.035), but unchanged in lobule X (10.4 ± 0.5 Hz/100 pA vs. 11.5 ± 1.1 Hz/100 pA, mut. vs. ctrl, t22=-0.95, p=0.354).
source: In line with the cell-attached recordings, in loss-of-function pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice, PC intrinsic excitability, quantified by the slope of firing rate versus current injection curve, was significantly reduced in lobules I-III (16.0 ± 1.0 Hz/100 pA vs. 19.2 ± 1.1 Hz/100 pA, mut. vs. ctrl, t32=-2.20, p=0.035), but unchanged in lobule X, compared with those of littermate controls (10.4 ± 0.5 Hz/100 pA vs. 11.5 ± 1.1 Hz/100 pA, mut. vs. ctrl, t22=-0.95, p=0.354) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Other physiological parameters in terms of holding current, amplitudes, half-widths and after-hyperpolarization amplitudes (AHPs), were not significantly affected in either lobules I-III or lobule X in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.
source: Other physiological parameters in terms of holding current, amplitudes, half-widths and after-hyperpolarization amplitudes (AHPs), were not significantly affected in either lobules I-III or lobule X (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In vivo, PCs in Z- lobules I-III of TRPC3Mwk/- mutants showed an increased simple spike firing rate (110.0 ± 22.6 Hz vs. 89.1 ± 15.3 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t60=-4.58, p<0.001), whereas the Z+ PCs were unaffected (50.6 ± 13.6 Hz vs. 45.3 ± 10.4 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t42=-1.47, p=0.148).
source: In vivo, in the presence of physiological inputs the PCs in Z– lobules I-III of TRPC3Mwk/- mutants showed an increased simple spike firing rate (110.0 ± 22.6 Hz vs. 89.1 ± 15.3 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t60=-4.58, p<0.001), whereas the Z+ PCs were unaffected (50.6 ± 13.6 Hz vs. 45.3 ± 10.4 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t42=-1.47, p=0.148).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: Z- PCs in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mutants featured a decreased simple spike firing rate (74.4 ± 18.6 Hz vs. 88.5 ± 17.4 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t54=2.88, p=0.006), but without changes in PCs of the Z+ lobule X (50.2 ± 15.5 Hz vs. 50.0 ± 12.9 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t54=-0.053, p=0.958).
source: Conversely, Z– PCs in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mutants featured a decreased simple spike firing rate (74.4 ± 18.6 Hz vs. 88.5 ± 17.4 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t54=2.88, p=0.006), but again without changes in PCs of the Z+ lobule X (50.2 ± 15.5 Hz vs. 50.0 ± 12.9 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t54=-0.053, p=0.958), all compared to those of their littermate controls (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: The ablation of TRPC3 did not decrease simple spike firing rate in the Z- PCs completely to levels of Z+ PCs (74.4 Hz vs. 50.0 Hz in Z- vs. Z+ of pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl, respectively).
source: Thus, here too, the ablation of TRPC3 did not decrease simple spike firing rate in the Z– PCs completely to levels of Z+ PCs (74.4 Hz vs. 50.0 Hz in Z– vs. Z+ of pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl, respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of firing rates between Z- and Z+ PCs in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.

claim: PCs in the pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice showed comparable CV and CV2 to controls for both Z- and Z+ modules in vivo.
source: Unlike in vitro, PCs in the pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice showed comparable CV and CV2 to controls for both Z– and Z+ modules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of firing regularity parameters shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The CV of simple spike ISI was prominently elevated in both Z- and Z+ modules in TRPC3Mwk/- mutants in vivo.
source: The CV of simple spike ISI was, however, prominently elevated in both Z– and Z+ modules in TRPC3Mwk/- mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), while the CV2 did not differ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of firing regularity parameters shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: In pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/- mice, the absence of TRPC3 attenuated the firing rate in Z- PCs (36.5 ± 23.2 Hz vs. 72.7 ± 26.5 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t28=3.99, p<0.001) and enhanced the irregularity (e.g. CV: 0.55 ± 0.16 vs. 0.44 ± 0.10, mut. vs. ctrl, t28=-2.27, p=0.031), without an effect on Z+ PCs (rate: 36.6 ± 19.5 Hz vs. 33.0 ± 9.8 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t21=-0.550, p=0.588; CV: 0.47 ± 0.22 vs. 0.56 ± 0.26, mut. vs. ctrl, t21=0.853, p=0.393).
source: Here, the absence of TRPC3 attenuated the firing rate (36.5 ± 23.2 Hz vs. 72.7 ± 26.5 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t28=3.99, p<0.001) and enhanced the irregularity (e.g. CV: 0.55 ± 0.16 vs. 0.44 ± 0.10, mut. vs. ctrl, t28=-2.27, p=0.031) of Z– PCs even more robustly, without an effect on Z+ PCs (rate: 36.6 ± 19.5 Hz vs. 33.0 ± 9.8 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t21=-0.550, p=0.588; CV: 0.47 ± 0.22 vs. 0.56 ± 0.26, mut. vs. ctrl, t21=0.853, p=0.393) (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B, cf Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-photon imaging-based targeted PC recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The similar firing rates of Z- and Z+ PCs lacking TRPC3 in targeted recordings supports the possibility that in some areas TRPC3 is solely responsible for the difference.
source: The similar firing rates of Z– and Z+ PCs lacking TRPC3 in these targeted recordings supports the possibility that in some areas TRPC3 is solely responsible for the difference and that further differentiation divides the zebrin-based populations into smaller subpopulations (Armstrong et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the firing rate data in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/- mice and is supported by a citation to Armstrong et al., 2001.

claim: Four weeks after tamoxifen treatment, pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice showed a virtually complete ablation of TRPC3 in PCs.
source: Four weeks after tamoxifen treatment, pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice showed a virtually complete ablation of TRPC3 in PCs (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In vivo recordings revealed that simple spike firing rates were affected in Z- PCs (from lobules I-III, 72.9 ± 9.1 Hz vs. 86.5 ± 10.9 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t53 = 5.05, p<0.001), but not Z+ PCs (lobule X, rate: 47.0 ± 11.6 Hz vs. 51.6 ± 13.4 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t44=1.21, p=0.234) of tamoxifen injected adult pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice.
source: In vivo recordings revealed that, again, simple spike firing rates were affected in Z– (from lobules I-III, 72.9 ± 9.1 Hz vs. 86.5 ± 10.9 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t53 = 5.05, p<0.001), but not Z+ PCs (lobule X, rate: 47.0 ± 11.6 Hz vs. 51.6 ± 13.4 Hz, mut. vs. ctrl, t44=1.21, p=0.234) of tamoxifen injected adult pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice (Figure 4G–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D), in a manner similar to that in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The TRPC3-dependent effects in zebrin-identified PCs are independent of cerebellar development or developmental compensation.
source: Taken together and combined with pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl data, these results indicate that the TRPC3-dependent effects in zebrin-identified PCs are independent of cerebellar development or developmental compensation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl and pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl data.

claim: Complex spike firing rates were higher in Z- than in Z+ PCs.
source: Complex spike firing rates were, similar to simple spike rates, higher in Z– than in Z+ PCs (Figure 5B), as shown previously (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo recordings shown in Figure 5B and is consistent with previous findings from Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: Chronic manipulations of TRPC3 activity, gain- and loss-of-function, in PCs predominantly affected complex spike firing rate in Z- PCs (TRPC3Mwk/-: t68=2.68, p=0.009; pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl: t54=2.50, p=0.016; pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/-: t28=3.49, p=0.002), but not Z+ PCs (TRPC3Mwk/-: t42=1.56, p=0.126; pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl: t54=1.41, p=0.164), except for that in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/- mice (t20 = 3.03, p=0.007).
source: Chronic manipulations of TRPC3 activity, gain- and loss-of-function, in PCs predominantly affected complex spike firing rate in Z– (TRPC3Mwk/-: t68=2.68, p=0.009; pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl: t54=2.50, p=0.016; pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/-: t28=3.49, p=0.002), but not Z+ PCs (TRPC3Mwk/-: t42=1.56, p=0.126; pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl: t54=1.41, p=0.164), except for that in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/- mice (t20 = 3.03, p=0.007) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Acute ablation of TRPC3 in pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice did not affect complex spike activity in terms of firing rate, CV, CV2 or pause in simple spikes following climbing fiber activation (CF-pause) in Z- PCs (rate: t53=-0.940, p=0.352).
source: Intriguingly, acute ablation of TRPC3 in pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice did not affect complex spike activity in terms of firing rate, CV, CV2 or pause in simple spikes following climbing fiber activation (CF-pause) in Z– PCs (rate: t53=-0.940, p=0.352) (Figure 5B bottom panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1J-L.

claim: In line with the lower simple spike firing rates in loss-of-function TRPC3 mutants, the CF-pause of pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl and pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/- mice were longer, selectively in Z- PCs.
source: In line with the lower simple spike firing rates in loss-of-function TRPC3 mutants, the CF-pause of pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl and pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/- mice were longer, selectively in Z– PCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CF-pause shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and I.

claim: Manipulation of TRPC3 activity changed the types of CS-SS responses most frequently in Z- PCs.
source: In addition, we found that manipulation of TRPC3 activity changed the types of CS-SS responses most frequently in Z– PCs (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CS-SS interaction patterns shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Z- PCs exhibited much more suppression in gain-of-function TRPC3Mwk/- mutants and vice versa more facilitation in loss-of-function pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/- mice, compared to those in their littermate controls.
source: Interestingly, Z– PCs exhibited much more suppression in gain-of-function TRPC3Mwk/- mutants and vice versa more facilitation in loss-of-function pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl;EAAT4GFP/- mice, compared to those in their littermate controls (Figure 5D), suggesting that Z– PCs partly compensate for the effects of TRPC3 manipulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CS-SS interaction patterns shown in Figure 5D and includes an inference about compensation.

claim: pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice did not show any overt signs of changes in development or weight, changes in module anatomy or connectivity or signs of any type of locomotion deficit.
source: pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice did not show any overt signs of changes in development or weight, changes in module anatomy or connectivity or signs of any type of locomotion deficit.
evidence: The claim is based on observational data from the pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.

claim: pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice could not be discriminated from control littermates by the percentage of different types of steps, including lower steps, also known as missteps.
source: pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice could not be discriminated from control littermates by the percentage of different types of steps, including lower steps, also known as missteps (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Erasmus Ladder behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Neither the gain (the ratio of eye movement to stimulus amplitude), nor the phase (timing of the response relative to input), differed significantly between pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mutants and littermate controls for OKR, VOR, and VVOR (all p>0.25).
source: Neither the gain (the ratio of eye movement to stimulus amplitude), nor the phase (timing of the response relative to input), differed significantly between pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mutants and littermate controls (all p>0.25) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by compensatory eye movement recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: When pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice were subjected to both out-of-phase and in-phase training paradigms, no significant deficit was observed in the VOR gain increase and VOR gain decrease, respectively (VOR increase, F = 0.012, p=0.913; VOR decrease, F = 0.252, p=0.621).
source: When pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice were subjected to both out-of-phase and in-phase training paradigms, we did not observe any significant deficit in the VOR gain increase and VOR gain decrease, respectively (VOR increase, F = 0.012, p=0.913; VOR decrease, F = 0.252, p=0.621) (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by VOR adaptation training data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: No difference was found between pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl and control littermate mice in the VOR phase over the training, nor in the increased OKR gain following the phase reversal training (VOR phase reversal, F = 0.006, p=0.942; OKR increase, F = 0.922, p=0.922).
source: Again, no difference was found between pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl and control littermate mice: neither in the VOR phase over the training (Figure 6H), nor in the increased OKR gain following the phase reversal training (VOR phase reversal, F = 0.006, p=0.942; OKR increase, F = 0.922, p=0.922)(Figure 6F, compare to Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by VOR phase reversal training data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6F and 6H.

claim: The L7-TPRC3KO mice showed significant deficits in eyeblink conditioning during the first week of training.
source: In contrast to VOR adaptation, the L7-TPRC3KO mice showed significant deficits in eyeblink conditioning during the first week of training (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by eyeblink conditioning data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: When subjected to longer periods of eyeblink conditioning training, pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice reached similar CR percentages, amplitudes and timing as controls.
source: However, when we subjected them to longer periods, they reached similar CR percentages, amplitudes and timing (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by eyeblink conditioning data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The delayed appearance of evoked conditioned responses in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice could not be explained by a deficit in the ability to close the eyelid, as the timing of the unconditioned response (UR) did not differ between mutant and control mice.
source: The delayed appearance of evoked conditioned responses could neither be explained by a deficit in the ability to close the eyelid, as the timing of the unconditioned response (UR) did not differ between mutant and control mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), nor by a lower level of locomotor activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which has previously been shown to impair eyeblink conditioning (Albergaria et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of UR timing shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and is consistent with previous findings from Albergaria et al., 2018.

claim: TRPC3 activity is selectively required to optimize the cerebellum-dependent learning behavior that is processed in a Z- module.
source: Thus, although TRPC3 is expressed in both regions underlying the cerebellum-dependent behavioral experiments tested here, TRPC3 activity is selectively required to optimize the cerebellum-dependent learning behavior that is processed in a Z– module (De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the behavioral data and is supported by a citation to De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015.

claim: The cellular heterogeneity and consequential differentiation in cellular activity also affects the behavior of the animals.
source: This indicates that the cellular heterogeneity and consequential differentiation in cellular activity also affects the behavior of the animals.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: Zebrin-negative PCs show a relatively high expression of TRPC3, which has a dominant impact on its electrophysiological features.
source: Here, we demonstrated that zebrin-negative PCs show a relatively high expression of TRPC3, which has a dominant impact on its electrophysiological features (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the combined data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Gain-of-function and loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding for TRPC3 selectively affected activity in the zebrin-negative modules and the motor behavior that is controlled by these modules.
source: Indeed, gain-of-function and loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding for TRPC3 selectively affected activity in the zebrin-negative modules and the motor behavior that is controlled by these modules.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the combined electrophysiological and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRPC3 is at least a major contributor to the increased firing rate of Z- PCs, but other factors putatively contribute as well.
source: Hence, TRPC3 is at least a major contributor to the increased firing rate of Z– PCs, but other factors putatively contribute as well.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that TRPC3 ablation does not completely eliminate the difference between Z- and Z+ PC firing rates.

claim: Although TRPC3 is present in all PCs, loss- and gain-of-function mutations selectively affected Z- PCs, suggesting that other proteins in the pathway leading to TRPC3 activation may be involved.
source: Although TRPC3 is present in all PCs, loss- and gain-of-function mutations selectively affected Z– PCs, suggesting that other proteins in the pathway leading to TRPC3 activation may be involved.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the selective effects of TRPC3 mutations on Z- PCs despite TRPC3 expression in all PCs.

claim: TRPC channels are calcium-permeable upon activation by phospholipase C or diacylglycerol and are widely expressed in the brain and critically involved in the development and maintenance of synaptic transmission.
source: TRPC channels, which are calcium-permeable upon activation by phospholipase C or diacylglycerol, are widely expressed in the brain and critically involved in the development and maintenance of synaptic transmission (Hartmann et al., 2008; Hartmann et al., 2011; Becker, 2014; Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRPC1 and TRPC3 are both prominently expressed in the cerebellum, but in PCs TRPC3 is most abundant.
source: TRPC1 and TRPC3 are both prominently expressed in the cerebellum, but in PCs TRPC3 is most abundant (Hartmann et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Hartmann et al., 2008.

claim: TRPC3 currents mediate the slow excitatory postsynaptic potential following activation of mGluR1b, which is expressed in a pattern complementary to that of zebrin.
source: In addition to its contribution to intrinsic activity, TRPC3 currents also mediate the slow excitatory postsynaptic potential following activation of mGluR1b, which is expressed in a pattern complementary to that of zebrin (Mateos et al., 2001; Hartmann et al., 2011; Ohtani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is the 'molecular machinery' involving mGluR1b activation combined with TRPC3 expression patterns, that drive the differential TRPC3 function.
source: Taken together, this suggests that it is in fact the 'molecular machinery' involving mGluR1b activation combined with TRPC3 expression patterns, that drive the differential TRPC3 function.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined expression patterns of TRPC3 and mGluR1b and the selective effects of TRPC3 mutations.

claim: mGluR1a is expressed by all PCs (estimated ratio 2:1 to mGluR1b).
source: In contrast to mGluR1b, mGluR1a is expressed by all PCs (estimated ratio 2:1 to mGluR1b) (Mateos et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Mateos et al., 2001.

claim: The metabotropic receptor mGluR1a is important for IP3-mediated calcium release, climbing fiber elimination as well as PF-PC LTD.
source: The metabotropic receptor mGluR1a is important for IP3-mediated calcium release, climbing fiber elimination as well as PF-PC LTD (Ohtani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Ohtani et al., 2014.

claim: mGluR1-dependent processes are hampered in zebrin-positive PCs by the expression of EAAT4.
source: Intriguingly, and in line with the concept of modular differentiation, mGluR1-dependent processes are hampered in zebrin-positive PCs by the expression of EAAT4 (Wadiche and Jahr, 2005), whereas zebrin-negative PCs selectively express PLCβ4 that works in concert with mGluR1a (Ohtani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to Wadiche and Jahr, 2005 and Ohtani et al., 2014.

claim: Zebrin-negative PCs selectively express PLCβ4 that works in concert with mGluR1a.
source: Intriguingly, and in line with the concept of modular differentiation, mGluR1-dependent processes are hampered in zebrin-positive PCs by the expression of EAAT4 (Wadiche and Jahr, 2005), whereas zebrin-negative PCs selectively express PLCβ4 that works in concert with mGluR1a (Ohtani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Ohtani et al., 2014.

claim: The differences in expression patterns may enhance the probability of PF-PC LTD in zebrin-negative PCs over that in zebrin-positive PCs, which is supported by experiments performed in P21 mice.
source: The differences in expression patterns may enhance the probability of PF-PC LTD in zebrin-negative PCs over that in zebrin-positive PCs, which is supported by experiments performed in P21 mice (Wadiche and Jahr, 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to Wadiche and Jahr, 2005.

claim: The reduced simple spike rate in zebrin-negative PCs leads to a lower complex spike rate in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.
source: The additional effects are particularly striking in the pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice, where the reduced simple spike rate in zebrin-negative PCs leads to a lower complex spike rate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed correlation between simple spike and complex spike rates in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.

claim: Lower simple spike rate results in reduced inhibition of the also inhibitory projection from the cerebellar nuclei to the inferior olive.
source: In principle, this could have been a direct olivocerebellar loop effect, as lower simple spike rate results in reduced inhibition of the also inhibitory projection from the cerebellar nuclei to the inferior olive (Chaumont et al., 2013; Witter et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about olivocerebellar loop circuitry supported by citations to Chaumont et al., 2013 and Witter et al., 2013.

claim: TRPC3Mwk/- mice exhibit a higher PC simple spike rate, but also a lower complex spike rate.
source: In contrast, TRPC3Mwk/- mice exhibit a higher PC simple spike rate, but also a lower complex spike rate.
evidence: The claim is based on the in vivo recording data from TRPC3Mwk/- mice.

claim: The unaltered complex spike rate of pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice suggests that there is a developmental component to the relationship between complex spikes and simple spikes.
source: The unaltered complex spike rate of pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice suggests that there is a developmental component to the relationship between complex spikes and simple spikes (Badura et al., 2013; White and Sillitoe, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl data and is supported by citations to Badura et al., 2013 and White and Sillitoe, 2017.

claim: TRPC3 is expressed in UBCs and inferior olivary neurons.
source: It should be noted that in some experiments we found that also the Z+ PCs were affected by TRPC3 mutations. In TRPC3Mwk/- mice the regularity of simple spikes and complex spikes was higher compared to controls. TRPC3 is expressed in UBCs and inferior olivary neurons (see also Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplements 1-2.

claim: UBCs are neurons that fire action potential with high regularity and provide mossy fiber input in lobule X, which indirectly drives PC simple spike activity.
source: UBCs are neurons that fire action potential with high regularity (Ruigrok et al., 2011) and provide mossy fiber input in lobule X, which -indirectly- drives PC simple spike activity (Nunzi et al., 2001), whereas inferior olivary neurons directly control the rate and regularity of complex spikes (De Zeeuw et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations to Ruigrok et al., 2011, Nunzi et al., 2001, and De Zeeuw et al., 2011.

claim: Inferior olivary neurons directly control the rate and regularity of complex spikes.
source: UBCs are neurons that fire action potential with high regularity (Ruigrok et al., 2011) and provide mossy fiber input in lobule X, which -indirectly- drives PC simple spike activity (Nunzi et al., 2001), whereas inferior olivary neurons directly control the rate and regularity of complex spikes (De Zeeuw et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by a citation to De Zeeuw et al., 2011.

claim: UBCs degenerate early in development in TRPC3Mwk/-.
source: UBCs degenerate early in development in TRPC3Mwk/-, while the effects of the mutation on inferior olivary neurons have not been described yet.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the TRPC3Mwk/- mouse model.

claim: TRPC3 mutations, through direct effects on inferior olivary neurons and/or indirect effects through the olivocerebellar loop, have an inhibiting effect on complex spike rates.
source: In general, in all conditions the complex spikes rate in Z– and Z+ appear to be significantly or trending towards lower values in mutant mice, except for those in inducible mice where the mutation occurred after development. This has two potential implications: 1) TRPC3 mutations, through direct effects on inferior olivary neurons and/or indirect effects through the olivocerebellar loop, have an inhibiting effect on complex spike rates, and 2) these effects are absent when the mutation is induced later in life.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pattern of complex spike rate changes across different TRPC3 mutant models.

claim: The effects of TRPC3 mutations on complex spike rates are absent when the mutation is induced later in life.
source: In general, in all conditions the complex spikes rate in Z– and Z+ appear to be significantly or trending towards lower values in mutant mice, except for those in inducible mice where the mutation occurred after development. This has two potential implications: 1) TRPC3 mutations, through direct effects on inferior olivary neurons and/or indirect effects through the olivocerebellar loop, have an inhibiting effect on complex spike rates, and 2) these effects are absent when the mutation is induced later in life.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that pcp2CreERT2;TRPC3fl/fl mice do not show changes in complex spike rates.

claim: Eyeblink conditioning requires a novel, well-timed eyelid movement to a previously unrelated, neutral stimulus, and has been linked to largely or completely zebrin-negative modules in the anterior cerebellum.
source: Eyeblink conditioning requires a novel, well-timed eyelid movement to a previously unrelated, neutral stimulus, and has been linked to largely or completely zebrin-negative modules in the anterior cerebellum (Hesslow, 1994; Mostofi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations to Hesslow, 1994 and Mostofi et al., 2010.

claim: The activity of the putative zebrin-negative PCs in the eyeblink conditioning area is relatively high at rest, in line with their zebrin identity, and a decrease in this high firing rate correlates to the eyeblink response.
source: The activity of the putative zebrin-negative PCs in this area is relatively high at rest, in line with their zebrin identity, and a decrease in this high firing rate correlates to the eyeblink response (Jirenhed et al., 2007; Johansson et al., 2014; ten Brinke et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations to Jirenhed et al., 2007, Johansson et al., 2014, and ten Brinke et al., 2015.

claim: VOR adaptation adjusts the amplitude of an existing reflex to optimize sensory processing using visual feedback and is controlled by the vestibulocerebellum, the flocculus in particular, which is classically considered to be zebrin-positive.
source: Conversely, VOR adaptation adjusts the amplitude of an existing reflex to optimize sensory processing using visual feedback and is controlled by the vestibulocerebellum, the flocculus in particular, which is classically considered to be zebrin-positive (Sanchez et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2014; cf Sugihara and Quy, 2007; Fujita et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations to Sanchez et al., 2002, Zhou et al., 2014, Sugihara and Quy, 2007, and Fujita et al., 2014.

claim: In unidirectional VOR gain increase, the change correlating with the adapted eye movement consisted of a potentiation, an increase, of the -at rest- lower PC firing rate.
source: In unidirectional VOR gain increase, we recently found that the change correlating with the adapted eye movement consisted of a potentiation, an increase, of the -at rest- lower PC firing rate (Voges et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Voges et al., 2017.

claim: The reduction in firing rate of zebrin-negative PCs may directly contribute to the impaired eyeblink conditioning in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.
source: Although our current study has its main focus on the differential contribution of TRPC3 at the cell and systems physiological level, it is tempting to speculate how the loss of TRPC3 in PCs results in an eyeblink conditioning phenotype without affecting VOR adaptation. The reduction in firing rate of zebrin-negative PCs may directly contribute to the impaired conditioning.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the mechanism underlying the eyeblink conditioning phenotype.

claim: The suppression of simple spike firing that generally correlates with the conditioned response might be occluded by the lower resting rate in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.
source: The suppression of simple spike firing that generally correlates with the conditioned response (ten Brinke et al., 2015) might be occluded by the lower resting rate in pcp2Cre;TRPC3fl/fl mice.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to ten Brinke et al., 2015.

claim: PF-PC LTD is in line with the simple spike suppression and blocking TRPC3 function completely abolishes this form of LTD.
source: Alternatively, PF-PC LTD could play a role as it is in line with the simple spike suppression and blocking TRPC3 function completely abolishes this form of LTD (Kim, 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Kim, 2013.

claim: Genetically ablating PF-PC LTD did not affect the ability to perform eyeblink conditioning successfully.
source: However, genetically ablating PF-PC LTD did not affect the ability to perform eyeblink conditioning successfully (Schonewille et al., 2011), arguing against an exclusive role for this form of plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Schonewille et al., 2011.

claim: Intrinsic excitability is increased after eyeblink conditioning.
source: Schreurs and colleagues demonstrated that intrinsic excitability is increased after eyeblink conditioning (Schreurs et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Schreurs et al., 1997.

claim: TRPC3 may also affect the adaptive increase of excitability, intrinsic plasticity, which is calcium-activated potassium channel function dependent, and thereby delays the expression of a conditioned blink response.
source: A third option could be that TRPC3 also affects the adaptive increase of excitability, intrinsic plasticity, which is calcium-activated potassium channel function dependent (Ohtsuki et al., 2012), and thereby delays the expression of a conditioned blink response.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to Ohtsuki et al., 2012.

claim: Trans-synaptic retrograde tracing using rabies virus from antagonist muscles demonstrated that there is no robust division in zebrin-negative and zebrin-positive strips, but that a partial segregation could not be excluded.
source: Trans-synaptic retrograde tracing using rabies virus from antagonist muscles demonstrated that there is no robust division in zebrin-negative and zebrin-positive strips, but that a partial segregation could not be excluded (Ruigrok et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Ruigrok et al., 2008.

claim: In the vestibulocerebellum of the pigeon, each movement direction is controlled by a set of zebrin-negative and zebrin-positive bands.
source: In the vestibulocerebellum of the pigeon, each movement direction is controlled by a set of zebrin-negative and zebrin-positive bands (Graham and Wylie, 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Graham and Wylie, 2012.

claim: Proper cerebellar function is based on the presence of (at least) two modi operandi that have distinct molecular machineries, with TRPC3 as one of the major contributing factors, so as to differentially control sensorimotor integration in downstream circuitries that require control with opposite polarity.
source: Altogether, this work demonstrates that proper cerebellar function is based on the presence of (at least) two modi operandi that have distinct molecular machineries, with TRPC3 as one of the major contributing factors, so as to differentially control sensorimotor integration in downstream circuitries that require control with opposite polarity.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the combined data presented in the manuscript.
